narrative:
**EOD MACRO-RISK BRIEF | 28 July 2026**

**Headline:**
Systemic risk remains High, driven by opaque leverage in credit markets, geopolitical weaponization of critical inputs, and structural vulnerabilities spanning finance, energy, and supply chains.

**Key Stories (No intraday changes reported):**

**High-band risks:** Private credit's opaque expansion (level 8) poses the greatest shock potential via hidden counterparty exposure. Japan's fiscal-JGB-carry nexus, China's deflationary spillover, critical minerals weaponization, AI power-grid bottlenecks, food-fertilizer fragility, and sea lanes/undersea cable disruption each remain systemic touch-points. 

**Elevated-band risks:** Treasury basis trades, developing-world debt, AI circular financing, CRE maturity walls, eurozone fragility, hidden consumer debt, ASML lithography chokepoint, and water underpricing all warrant continued monitoring.

**Watch closest:** Private credit's opaque expansion—level 8—remains the highest-intensity risk; opacity prevents real-time contagion assessment and magnifies tail-event probability.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: The Fitch PCDR at 6.0% TTM through May 2026 is the most recent confirmed Fitch print under the rubric's required methodology anchor (inclusive of distressed exchanges/LMEs); a LinkedIn post title suggests a possible July 2026 Fitch print of 5.2% but the full report is inaccessible and cannot be verified, so the confirmed May 2026 reading is retained per rubric rules. The sustained record-high rate, driven by ~94% distressed-exchange composition, confirms acute private credit stress without a direct funding-market transmission signal in public repo/SOFR data as of this date.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings' U.S. Private Credit Default Rate (PCDR), inclusive of distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises, remained at a record high of 6.0% for the trailing-twelve-month period through May 2026, per Fitch report posted June 15, 2026 (corroborated by LSTA commentary page and eprofitguard.com July 2026 credit outlook). The April 2026 print also read 6.0% (Fitch, posted May 18, 2026).

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index (count-based, excludes most distressed exchanges): 2.73% in Q1 2026, up from 1.84% two quarters prior
Fitch PCDR possibly dropped to 5.2% for a period ending June or July 2026 per unverified LinkedIn post title - could not confirm from accessible sources
Moody's: distressed restructurings accounted for ~65% of all 2025 private credit defaults; excluding them yields headline rates of 1.6%-4.7%

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric threshold for level 2 is >=3 of the largest funds OR combined gated AUM >$100bn; at least 6-8 named major funds across Q1-Q2 2026 enforced caps simultaneously, with BCRED alone at $82bn and HLEND at $26bn easily exceeding the $100bn AUM threshold without counting the others. No corroborating SOFR-EFFR or MOVE spike to systemic levels, but Blue Owl stock -33% YTD and Moody's flagging first-ever net outflow from non-traded BDCs confirm this is structural gating at scale, not a single isolated event.
items.fact: In Q1-Q2 2026, >= 6 named major private credit/BDC funds enforced quarterly repurchase caps: Blue Owl OBDC II (permanently gated Feb 19, ~$1.6bn), BlackRock HLEND ($26bn, 5% cap vs 9.3% requests Q1), Blackstone BCRED ($82bn, capped at 5% in Q2 after 10% requests), Morgan Stanley North Haven (5% cap vs 10.9% requests Q1), Cliffwater CCLFX ($33bn, 5% cap vs 17% requests Q2), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (5% cap vs 16.8% requests Q1), Blue Owl OCIC ($34bn, 5% cap vs 18.8% requests Q2), Golub Capital PCF (5% cap vs 8.5% Q2). Bloomberg (Jul 2, 2026), Congress.gov CRS IN12674 (Mar 2026), Investing.com (Jun 4, 2026).

dissent.view: CAIA and iCapital argue funds are 'operating as designed' and that caps are contractual features rather than distress gates, implying the rubric overstates severity

Benzinga/Moody's note that 'NAV BDCs have continued to provide liquidity without imposing redemption gates' for some funds, and several managers (Blackstone Q1, Oaktree) expanded caps above 5% to honor all requests

items.label: SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)
items.rationale: The rubric scores 1 for 'an official extension granted OR exemptive-relief requests pending': both conditions are met — the Feb 2025 extension is the first official extension, and SIFMA's inter-affiliate and IIB non-U.S. exemptive-relief requests were formally pending before the SEC as of Apr-May 2026. There is no evidence of a second deadline extension (which would score 2), so the score is capped at 1.
items.fact: On Feb 25 2025, the SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year to Dec 31 2026 (cash) and Jun 30 2027 (repo) — a first official extension (SEC Release No. 34-102487; sec.gov, Feb 25 2025). As of Apr 17 2026, the SEC published SIFMA's pending exemptive-relief requests (inter-affiliate exemption expansion and extraterritorial non-U.S. participant exemption), with a May 29 2026 public comment deadline, and open scoping issues for non-U.S. participants remain unresolved per the TBAC Q1-2 2026 charge document (home.treasury.gov, May 29 2026). No second formal deadline extension has been announced.

dissent.view: DTCC/Risk.net (Mar 2026) characterise infrastructure as ready and compliance path as clear, implying on-track sentiment closer to 0; however the prior formal extension and live exemptive-relief requests objectively satisfy rubric level 1 regardless of readiness optimism.

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Multiple TBAC/SEC/SIFMA sources confirm the December 2026 cash and June 2027 repo deadlines remain in place (no extension = not a '2'), but two material exemptive relief requests (inter-affiliate and extraterritorial) were still pending or only partially resolved as of late June 2026, a legal documentation backlog persists, and the SIFMA/DTCC Nov-2025 pulse survey flagged that unresolved issues by early 2026 would impair readiness—squarely meeting the rubric's FRICTION criteria of 'pending exemptive relief' and 'documentation backlog'.
items.fact: TBAC Q2 2026 presentation (May 2026) states: 'Largest challenge from an implementation standpoint continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with the bilateral agreements between participants' and 'it is possible that clearing will not be available to all participants in all regions by the deadline.' As of April 17, 2026, SIFMA's inter-affiliate exemptive relief request remained open for public comment (SEC Commissioner Uyeda update, Apr 20 2026); the IIB extraterritorial exemptive relief comment period was also reopened. On June 18, 2026 the SEC granted only conditional exemptive relief for private fund captive clearing subsidiaries. No deadline extension has been announced as of the as-of date.

dissent.view: Nov 2025 SIFMA/DTCC pulse survey found 71% of U.S. respondents 'very familiar' with changes and characterised domestic readiness as 'net positive', which could support a '0' reading for U.S.-domestic participants

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth rates (84%+ YoY at MSFT, >100% YoY at GOOGL in Q2) materially exceed AI-revenue growth rates, satisfying the 'capex exceeds AI-revenue growth' condition; however, AI revenue is still strongly accelerating YoY (GOOGL Cloud +82%, MSFT AI +123%) and accelerating QoQ (GOOGL Cloud 63%->82%), with no hyperscaler cutting its AI-revenue outlook, so Score 2 conditions are not met.
items.fact: Alphabet Q2 2026 (reported 2026-07-22): Google Cloud revenue +82% YoY to $24.8B, accelerating from +63% in Q1; Q2 capex $44.9B (>2x YoY), with full-year 2026 capex guidance raised to $195-$205B from $180-$190B; free cash flow -$5.9B. Microsoft Q3 FY2026 (reported 2026-04-29): AI revenue run rate $37B +123% YoY, capex $30.88B +84% YoY, full-year 2026 capex guided ~$190B. CreditSights estimates combined Big-5 hyperscaler capex ~$750B for 2026, +67% YoY. Sources: finance.yahoo.com/Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings (2026-07-22); geekwire.com/Microsoft Q3 FY2026 (2026-04-30); know.creditsights.com (2026-07).

dissent.view: Sequoia's David Cahn estimated a ~$600B annual gap between AI infrastructure spending and AI ecosystem revenue in 2025, implying the gap may be more severe (closer to Score 2) when measured against total AI ecosystem revenue rather than hyperscaler cloud/AI segment revenue alone

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: 30+ DPD rose 29 bps YoY — above zero but far below the 100 bps SPIKING threshold — and sector charge-offs (~1.83%) remain well under the 3% contained ceiling and the 5% SPIKING ceiling, squarely mapping to rubric level 1 (RISING, charge-offs contained).
items.fact: Affirm FQ3 2026 (qtr ended Mar 31 2026): 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans ex-Peloton/Pay-in-X = 2.8%, up 29 bps YoY; allowance for credit losses 6.0% of LHFI (up from 5.7% YoY); BNPL sector charge-off rate per Richmond Fed/CFPB = 1.83% (2023, latest reported). Source: Affirm FQ3 2026 Earnings Supplement (investors.affirm.com, May 7 2026); Richmond Fed EB-26-05 (Mar 5 2026).

dissent.view: Finsee analyst flags allowance spike (5.4% seq to 6.0%) as 'contradicting management narrative' and warrants strict monitoring, implying potential deterioration beyond management characterisation of 'very stable'
Richmond Fed (Mar 2026) notes 'indicative evidence' of rising late-payment behaviour since 2023 but finds no clear systemic stress in broader consumer credit markets

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric asks for the latest CMBS office delinquency rate as a percent from Trepp; the most recent Trepp-attributed office-specific figure is ~11.7% (Jan 2026), with Trepp's June 2026 report confirming office delinquencies continued to rise — placing the current Trepp office rate modestly above 11.7%, but no precise June figure was publicly available. KBRA's methodology yields a higher figure (~12.8%), recorded as dissent.
items.fact: Trepp reported office CMBS delinquency at ~11.7% in January 2026 (per Trepp data cited by multiple outlets); Trepp's June 2026 overall CMBS report states office delinquencies 'increased' further in June vs May, but the precise Trepp office sub-rate for June 2026 was not publicly quoted in available sources. KBRA (a competing authoritative source) reported office delinquency at 13.9% in January 2026 and 12.8% in February 2026 (BusinessWire, 2026-02-27). The Trepp June 2026 overall rate was 7.35% (MBA Newslink, 2026-07-08).

dissent.view: KBRA office CMBS delinquency rate was 13.9% in January 2026 and fell to 12.8% in February 2026 — materially higher than Trepp's figure, reflecting KBRA's rated-universe methodology
S&P Global Ratings noted the office CMBS rate 'surpasses 10.5%' in January 2026, lower than both Trepp and KBRA readings, reflecting S&P's rated-universe scope

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: A named borrower (CoreWeave) faces a documented $4.2bn 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-collateralized debt with declining collateral values, and banks are reported offloading AI data-centre debt tranches at a discount - both qualifying signs under rubric level 1. However, CoreWeave has actively managed the wall through oversubscribed bond sales and new IG-rated facilities with no confirmed default, failed refinancing, or distressed exchange, so level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: CoreWeave carried a '$4.2 billion refinancing wall due in 2026 on debt that predates the Meta structure' against GPUs that 'have depreciated substantially since the loans were written' (davefriedman.substack.com, Apr 19 2026); separately, banks were reported to be trying to offload AI data-centre debt as exposure mounts (resultsense.com, May 6 2026). CoreWeave addressed part of this wall via a $3.75bn high-yield bond refinancing (~9% coupon, heavily oversubscribed) and a March 2026 $8.5bn DDTL 4.0 rated A3/A(low) by Moody's/DBRS - no confirmed default or distressed exchange has been reported.

dissent.view: CoreWeave's $8.5bn DDTL 4.0 (March 2026) priced at investment-grade (A3/Moody's) and its May $2bn bond was 'heavily oversubscribed', suggesting orderly refinancing rather than stress
Nvidia has stepped in as a backstop guarantor for neocloud GPU offtakes in mid-2026, reducing idiosyncratic refinancing risk across the sector

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: Thirteen states with documented non-renewal pressure falls squarely in the 5-15 state RISING band; FL stabilization and the AM Best national-outlook upgrade to stable preclude the ACCELERATING threshold, and no confirmed top-10 insurer full state exit for homeowners occurred in 2026.
items.fact: A June 2026 climate-risk tracker (climatecosmos.com, June 18 2026) identifies 13 US states with active homeowner non-renewal waves; named states include FL, CA, LA, TX, CO, GA, OK. NAIC MCAS 2024 data shows FL at 3.35% and CA at 3.18% non-renewal rates (highest in nation). AM Best lifted the national HO market outlook to stable (Dec 2025) but FL and CA state-segment outlooks remain 'materially weaker than the national average' (leadgen-economy.com, June 25 2026). Florida Citizens depopulated from 1.42M to ~390K policies by Jan 2026, signaling partial FL stabilization. NAIC 2026 Homeowners Market Data Call submissions due June 15 2026; aggregate public report targeted early 2027.

dissent.view: AM Best upgraded the US homeowners segment outlook to stable in Dec 2025, suggesting the peak of market exits may have passed nationally

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Zero failures in the trailing 6 months where CRE/RE was formally cited as a contributing cause by regulators, falling short of the >=3 threshold or >$10B asset failure needed for CLUSTER (score=2). However, the FDIC 2026 Risk Review and ongoing regulatory flagging of CRE concentration at community/regional banks constitute active supervisory statements citing CRE concentration, satisfying the ISOLATED prong of >=1 public enforcement action/supervisory statement citing regional-bank CRE concentration. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: Four US banks failed in 2026 YTD per FDIC (last updated July 17, 2026): Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust ($261M, Jan 30), Community Bank & Trust - West Georgia ($288M, May 2026), Kentland Federal S&L ($3.7M, Jul 10), Small Business Bank ($73M, Jul 17). None had CRE concentration formally cited as cause by FDIC/Fed/OCC; Metropolitan Capital had a tangential real-estate loan per Bisnow (Feb 2, 2026) but regulators cited 'unsafe/unsound conditions and impaired capital.' The FDIC 2026 Risk Review (fdic.gov) and ongoing federal flagging of banks with CRE >300% of capital constitute active supervisory statements on regional-bank CRE concentration. No coordinated interagency emergency CRE facility announced. Source: FDIC Failed Bank List (fdic.gov, updated Jul 17 2026); American Banker (Jul 17 2026); Bisnow (Feb 2 2026).

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the latest published 60+ day subprime auto delinquency rate as a percent; Fitch's March 2026 index reading of 6.11% is the most recent monthly data point with explicit sourcing, mapping directly to the rubric. Confidence is medium because the figure comes via a secondary report (Auto Remarketing) citing Fitch rather than a direct Fitch URL, and April-June 2026 Fitch index data has not surfaced in available search results.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS 60-day delinquency index declined to 6.11% in March 2026 (February collection period), aided by seasonal tax-refund effects, after hitting a record 6.90% in January 2026; reported in Auto Remarketing citing Fitch Vehicle Depreciation Report, May 21 2026.

dissent.view: TradingEconomics (sourcing Fitch Auto ABS Indices, last updated April 2026) shows 'Actual: 6.80%' as the most recent figure, implying February 2026 was the latest data in their feed at time of update
Motley Fool / Yahoo Finance articles (July 2026) characterize the rate as 'around 6.8%' at the start of 2026, likely referencing the January-February peak rather than the March seasonal dip

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: Lecornu is governing but holds no working majority, has survived multiple no-confidence votes only through concessions, and passed the budget without a direct parliamentary majority vote — squarely meeting rubric band 1 (fragile minority/hung parliament surviving no-confidence votes). No dissolution or PM resignation has been recorded after Sep 2025 Bayrou collapse; Lecornu's government is functional but precarious.
items.fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's minority government survived two no-confidence votes on 2 Feb 2026, allowing the overdue 2026 budget to pass; Reuters (via AOL, 2 Feb 2026) described this as 'a period of relative stability for Lecornu's weak minority government.' The National Assembly remains a three-bloc hung parliament with no party holding an absolute majority, and the government has repeatedly relied on Socialist acquiescence and Article 49.3-type budget manoeuvres to survive.

dissent.view: Bloomberg (9 Jan 2026) reported Finance Minister Lescure warning that a further government fall could trigger snap elections/dissolution — indicating the government's hold remains contested, though no dissolution has been executed as of latest data.

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: Equable's 85.0% is the most comprehensive and most recently published aggregate for U.S. public pensions (July 23, 2026), covering 253 systems and representing the broadest national funded ratio in use. The Milliman PPFI reading of 87.6% (April 30, 2026, top 100 plans only) is directionally consistent, providing corroboration at a slightly higher level due to its focus on the largest plans.
items.fact: Equable Institute State of Pensions 2026 (published July 23, 2026): 'The national funded ratio is projected to reach 85.0% in FY2026, up 3.9 points from 81.2% in 2025 — the fourth consecutive year of improvement and the best level since 2009.' (253 statewide and municipal systems, all 50 states + D.C.)

dissent.view: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index: PPFI funded ratio at 87.6% as of April 30, 2026, for the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans (assets $6.009T vs. liabilities $6.860T)
Equable Institute year-end update to State of Pensions 2025 (Jan 8, 2026): aggregate funded ratio at 82.5% for end of calendar year 2025

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: One new IMF arrangement (Ukraine EFF, Feb 2026) falls within the trailing 6-month window; rubric RISING requires 1-2 new IMF arrangements OR a single missed coupon/standstill, satisfied by Ukraine alone. No confirmed new EM missed coupon or additional new program was found, so the threshold for CLUSTER (>=3) is not met.
items.fact: IMF Executive Board approved a new US$8.1bn EFF arrangement for Ukraine on 26 Feb 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/02/26/pr-26066-ukraine-imf-executive-board-approves-usd-8point1-billion-under-an-eff-arrangement). No other new EM sovereign IMF arrangements or missed coupons were confirmed in the Jan 27-Jul 27 2026 window; ongoing reviews (Egypt EFF, Argentina EFF, Gambia ECF, Côte d'Ivoire EFF) are completions of pre-existing programs approved before the window.

dissent.view: Ukraine's bilateral official debt standstill extension by G7/Paris Club creditors could be characterised as a new standstill action within the window, which independently satisfies RISING without counting the IMF program; however it is an extension of a pre-existing standstill, not a new one, so it does not change the band.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: All primary regulatory sources (TPR, ESMA) confirm materially improved buffers (~300 bps), sharply reduced market size and leverage, and no active episode of margin stress or forced selling in 2026; the rubric condition for score 1 requires a regulator to flag active LDI/pension liquidity risk or an unresolved margin-call episode, neither of which is present. ESMA's residual tail-risk caveat for a subset of funds under a large shock is a stress-test finding, not a live crisis flag, keeping the reading at 0.
items.fact: TPR's Market Oversight report (data to March 2025) states the LDI market has shrunk from ~£1.5tn to ~£0.7tn, rate buffers have been raised to ~300 bps (vs ~150 bps pre-2022), and daily volatility in leveraged LDI assets is more than 50% lower than end-2021. ESMA's June 2026 liquidity stress test paper confirms the liquidity shortfall across LDI funds fell from €9bn to €3bn between 2022 and end-2024, while noting a subset of funds 'might still face challenges' under a large rate shock. No TPR, BoE or ESMA alert of an active margin-call episode or forced selling has been issued in 2026. (Sources: TPR Market Oversight report thepensionsregulator.gov.uk; ESMA paper ESMA50-1949966494-4208, June 2026; Reuters/MarketScreener Jan 2025 gilt sell-off piece, which describes cash calls being met 'in an orderly way'.)

dissent.view: ESMA June 2026 stress test notes 'a subset of funds might still face challenges in meeting liquidity demands in case of a large interest rate shock', implying residual tail vulnerability even if no live crisis

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: No new sovereign asset seizure has been executed, ruling out level 2. Active official rhetoric and announced (but not yet operationally live) BRICS Pay non-dollar settlement agreements place this squarely at level 1 (TALK): new settlement system launches announced/targeted but not yet in full operational deployment.
items.fact: As of July 2026, no new sovereign reserve seizure/confiscation has been executed — Russian assets (~€210–300bn) remain frozen (not confiscated) with EU's largest holders (Belgium, France, Germany) still opposing outright seizure per European Parliament EPRS Briefing (Sep 2025) and Brookings (Jun 2025). Separately, BRICS Pay is officially targeted for a pilot launch at the India BRICS summit (late 2026), but the system's own tracker (bricspayment.ru) notes it 'remains in the planning and early-pilot stage' with full operational status pegged to 2030 by Russia's Deputy FM; EBC Financial Group (Apr 13, 2026) confirms no live BRICS common currency or operationally deployed system.

dissent.view: Some non-primary sources (watcher.guru, informedclearly.com) characterize BRICS Pay as already 'operational' in 2026 with 67% intra-bloc local currency trade — overstating actual deployment status relative to official BRICS and BIS sources.

Modern Diplomacy (Dec 2025) described EU as 'plotting permanent freeze' of Russian billions under Article 122, implying imminent escalation to confiscation — but this has not been executed as of mid-2026.

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report worsened the depletion date and the long-term financing gap materially deteriorated, and active bipartisan reform legislation is being debated in Congress — squarely matching rubric band 1 (DEBATE). No automatic cut has been triggered and no legislation enacting cuts has been enacted, so band 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: The 2026 SSA Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026) projects OASI trust fund depletion in Q4 2032 — one quarter earlier than the 2025 report — with only 78% of scheduled benefits payable thereafter; the 75-year actuarial deficit widened to 4.42% of taxable payroll from 3.82%. No benefit cuts have been enacted or automatically triggered. Multiple bipartisan reform bills (Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R.9187; PROMISE Act, introduced July 2026) are in debate but none enacted. Source: https://www.ssa.gov/oact/trsum/ (June 9, 2026).

dissent.view: AARP and some analysts emphasise that the combined OASDI date is unchanged at 2034 (not 2032), potentially understating urgency; OASI-only 2032 date is the load-bearing figure used by SSA trustees and most authoritative commentators.

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
items.rationale: The rubric asks for the latest published USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent; the most recent IMF COFER release (Q3 2025, Dec 22 2025) places that figure at 56.92%, mapping directly to the rubric. A third-party tracker (coferdata.com) shows 56.77%, a ~0.15pp discrepancy likely reflecting a post-release revision, recorded as dissent. [vintage guard: new read is 2025Q3 data but the prior applied value was 2026Q1 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: IMF COFER Q3 2025 data (released Dec 22, 2025): USD share of global FX reserves edged lower to 56.92%, per Reuters citing IMF data (globalbankingandfinance.com, Dec 22 2025). IMF data.imf.org confirms total reserves rose to $13.0 trillion in 2025Q3; starting Q3 2025 IMF eliminated the 'unallocated' category, covering 100% of world FX reserves.

dissent.view: coferdata.com tracker shows USD share at 56.77% for the latest quarter, ~0.15pp below the 56.92% reported by Reuters citing the Dec 22 2025 IMF COFER release, possibly reflecting a minor post-publication revision

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The rubric requires reporting the signed NBS figure exactly; +4.1% YoY is a sharp positive move representing a cost-push inflation signal that exports input-cost pressure to trading partners. The engine scores on magnitude of move, not sign; +4.1% is the largest reading since mid-2022 per corroborating sources.
items.fact: NBS official English press release (stats.gov.cn, 2026-07-10): 'In June 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 4.1% year on year and decreased by 0.3% month on month.'

dissent.view: MT Newswires/iTiger headline dated 07-09 claims 'PPI declined 3.6% on year in June' - this is clearly a misdated/recycled item from a prior deflation episode (likely June 2024) and contradicts the NBS official release directly; no current market signal supports ongoing deflation.

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Multiple corroborating sources across Q1-Q2 2026 consistently place the ex-China heavy rare earth (dysprosium/terbium oxide) price premium at approximately 4-7x the Chinese domestic benchmark, with the modal and most-cited figure at ~5x; the rubric calls for a single multiple so 5.0 is the best-supported central estimate. Market volume signals (Chinese HREE shipments down ~50% per customs data) confirm the price bifurcation is real and not a data artifact.
items.fact: Ucore Rare Metals (Barchart/Newsfile, Feb 23 2026): 'dysprosium oxide prices in China recently increased to over $200 per kg, with ex-China pricing more than 5 times that, at $1,000/kg'; corroborated by Benchmark Minerals (March 24 2026) reporting 4.4x in 2025 rising toward 8.3x by 2027, and Oregon Group (June 10 2026) citing Argus data showing dysprosium ~$1,450/kg ex-China vs ~$209/kg domestic China (~7x). Rareearthexchanges (June 5 2026) shows terbium ~$4,500-4,700/kg ex-China vs ~$914-923/kg domestic China (~5x).

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: Both sides enacted new measures within the 3-month window: the US introduced major new controls legislation (MATCH Act) targeting DUV lithography and initiated compliance inquiries; China enacted formal countermeasure regulations (April extraterritorial-jurisdiction rules + June outbound-investment regulations with penalty authority) and launched legal retaliation via the Wingtech/Nexperia lawsuit — meeting the rubric definition of level 2 (RETALIATION: target country enacts countermeasures/legal retaliation). Market signal is corroborated by ASML's China revenue share falling from 33% in 2025 to ~19-20% in Q1/full-year 2026 guidance.
items.fact: Within the trailing 3 months (Apr–Jul 2026): (1) US side — the bipartisan MATCH Act was introduced ~2 Apr 2026 targeting DUV immersion lithography exports to China (CNBC, 7 Apr 2026); US Commerce Secretary Lutnick began private meetings with ASML executives in Apr 2026 over suspected EUV diversion to China (Asia Times, ~14 Jul 2026). (2) China side — Beijing promulgated 'Regulations on Countering Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction by Foreign States' in April 2026, explicitly empowering Chinese authorities to prohibit firms such as ASML from complying with US FDP Rules (JustSecurity/MoFo, ~14 Jul 2026); China's State Council published 'Regulations on Outbound Investment' on 1 Jun 2026, including countermeasures and penalties for foreign restrictions deemed discriminatory against Chinese entities (Morrison Foerster, Jul 2026); Chinese semiconductor firm Wingtech sued Dutch subsidiary Nexperia in a Chinese court in May 2026 for ~US$1.2 bn over Dutch restrictive measures. Primary sources: CNBC reuters.com Apr 7 2026; JustSecurity Jul 14 2026; Morrison Foerster Jul 2026.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (Mar 2026) characterises the Trump White House as having 'traded loud escalation for quiet enforcement', approving higher-tier chip exports and suspending further restrictions — implying a partial de-escalation that could support a level-1 rather than level-2 reading on the US side.

CNBC (Jun 22 2026) reports China's trade curbs on US Pentagon-listed firms are 'largely symbolic' with 'little or no meaningful business exposure in China', suggesting Chinese countermeasures may not rise to material retaliation.

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
items.rationale: Hormuz transits are at ~3-17% of the ~88/day pre-crisis baseline (well under the 25% threshold), and the corroborating oil-price signal — Brent at $89-100/bbl, up ~40% in July — is fully consistent with a near-closure. No ceasefire, convoy workaround, or MOU is currently operative at Hormuz, satisfying the rubric's condition to assign 2 rather than capping at 1.
items.fact: Lloyd's List Intelligence tracked only 78 Hormuz transits July 13-20 vs. 174 the prior week (USNI News, 2026-07-24); PortWatch recorded 15 transits on 2026-07-19 vs. a pre-crisis baseline of ~88/day (straits.live, 2026-07-26); Kpler data shows just 3 transits/day July 22-24 (discoveryalert.com.au, 2026-07-25). Brent crude hit ~$96-100/bbl week of July 23-26 (TradingEconomics, 2026-07-26; CNN, 2026-07-23). Red Sea: Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and struck two Saudi oil tankers circa July 24 (CSMonitor, 2026-07-24). No functioning convoy workaround or ceasefire is in effect at Hormuz; the June 14 MOU ceasefire collapsed after fighting resumed July 7-8 (IEA July 2026 report).

dissent.view: Military-verified data (vs. AIS-only tracking) shows ~14 vessels transiting on some days, suggesting the strait is not physically zero-traffic — more 'severely contested' than legally closed
IEA July 2026 report notes a partial flow resumption in June under the interim ceasefire, implying the situation was briefly contested (1) before re-escalating

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: Six or more new discrete major-economy measures in 3 months clears the rubric threshold of >=4; the US forced-labour Section 301 round (12.5% across 60 economies including China) constitutes a broad tariff round >=10% across a sector, and the EU steel safeguard is a broad sector instrument — mapping unambiguously to level 2 (ESCALATING).
items.fact: In the trailing ~3 months (May–July 27 2026), at least 6 distinct new major-economy trade measures targeting China were enacted or took effect: (1) US Section 301 forced-labour tariff of 12.5% on China effective July 24 2026 (USTR/dimerco.com, July 24 2026); (2) EU definitive anti-dumping duties on passenger-car and light-lorry tyres from China, published July 7 2026 (policy.trade.ec.europa.eu); (3) EU steel-sector safeguard regulation targeting Chinese overcapacity, in force July 1 2026 (policy.trade.ec.europa.eu); (4) EU definitive anti-dumping duties on adipic acid from China at 29.1%–42.3%, May 5 2026 (EC/Institute of New Europe); (5) EU provisional anti-dumping duties on spunbond polyester nonwovens from China at 45.6%–50%, May 14 2026 (EU Reg. 2026/1063 via catts.eu); (6) EU definitive anti-dumping duty on woven/stitched glass fibre materials from China, EU Reg. 2026/1203, June 2026 (catts.eu). UK boom-lift AD/AS investigation with registration measures also active. Parallel US-China truce (October 2025 one-year extension) nominally covers reciprocal tariffs but did not prevent new Section 301 forced-labour round.

dissent.view: US-China October 2025 one-year truce nominally suspends reciprocal IEEPA tariffs until November 2026, suggesting a managed truce rather than full escalation; Polymarket consensus as of late June 2026 indicated ongoing managed-trade frameworks from the May 2026 Trump-Xi Beijing summit

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: All three SLOWING triggers fire simultaneously: licensing is whitelist-based (named producers/end-users only, not general blanket), statutory processing exceeds 30 days (45 working days), and new categories were added to the control list in the trailing 3 months (Jan 2026). No evidence of categorical country-wide denial or full suspension that would justify a '2'. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: MOFCOM general licences issued Dec 2025 cover only named producers (JL Mag, Yunsheng, San Huan) shipping to named end-users — not blanket coverage; statutory review window is 45 working days (~9 weeks) under the Dec 2024 Dual-Use Regulations; samarium/gadolinium/lutetium compounds added to the export licensing catalogue Jan 1 2026; and in June 2026 China added MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to its export control list barring approvals for those entities. Sources: Reuters/Tom's Hardware Dec 2 2025; gettransport.com (MOFCOM statutory 45-day target); Certivo/Andersen Institute Jan 2026 catalogue; Morgan Lewis July 2026.

dissent.view: Rare Earth Exchanges / multi-institutional analysis (Apr 2026) reports licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms, suggesting functional near-freeze conditions closer to a '2' for certain geographies.

CSIS (May 2026) documents highly volatile month-to-month flows and US imports never recovering to pre-restriction levels, implying the regime is more restrictive in practice than the formal architecture suggests.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)
items.rationale: The rubric scores EXTREME (2) when <10% of leading-edge (<=3nm) capacity is outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab exists. As of today, 100% of <=3nm capacity remains in Taiwan; the only overseas advanced node (Arizona 4nm) does not qualify under the rubric's <=3nm threshold, and no <=3nm fab outside Taiwan is in production.
items.fact: As of July 2026, TSMC has zero operational <=3nm capacity outside Taiwan. The sole overseas advanced fab — Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 — runs 4nm at an estimated ~10,000-20,000 wspm. Arizona Phase 2 (3nm) completed construction but begins tool installation Q3 2026 with volume production targeted H2 2027; Kumamoto Fab 2 (3nm) targets 2028. Taiwan hosts all <=3nm volume production: ~180,000 wspm at 3nm and ~90,000-100,000 wspm at 2nm, per TSMC Q1 2026 earnings (April 2026, focustaiwan.tw/trendforce.com) and CNBC/TechTimes Q2 2026 reporting (July 2026).

dissent.view: Some sources treat Arizona 4nm as 'leading-edge' diversification and note TSMC profits in Arizona/Kumamoto as evidence diversification is underway, potentially warranting a HIGH (1) read if the rubric threshold were relaxed to <=5nm.

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Two-day live-fire drill in the Taiwan Strait with official navigation warnings issued maps squarely to Rubric 1 (large-scale assertive activity/drills without kinetic clash or blockade). No price or volume signal indicative of a full blockade was reported, and no named large-scale encirclement exercise (e.g. 'Joint Sword' or 'Justice Mission' class) was announced, capping the read at 1 rather than 2.
items.fact: Reuters reported on 23 July 2026: 'China began two days of live-fire drills from Thursday in some parts of the Taiwan Strait near the shores of its southeastern province of Fujian,' confirmed by a Zhangzhou Maritime Safety Administration navigation warning. The drills ran 0600-1800 CST on 23-24 July and coincided with wider coastal military activity from the Bohai Sea to the South China Sea. No blockade, kinetic clash, or full mobilisation was reported. PLA ADIZ sortie volumes had been trending toward the pre-Lai baseline in early-to-mid July before this drill. (Reuters/SCMP/Epoch Times, 23-24 Jul 2026)

dissent.view: Epoch Times sources suggest the drills may reflect short-notice political-loyalty testing rather than routine signalling, and note a broader simultaneous multi-region exercise footprint, implying higher operational significance than a standalone coastal range event.

items.label: Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)
items.rationale: The SMW5 fault (July 2, 2026) constitutes a single cable incident causing active connectivity degradation but is not confirmed as a complete, unrepaired severing; this maps to rubric level 1 (THREATENED / single incident). No current unrepaired confirmed major cut is documented for July 2026, and the Hormuz threat posture (AGBI, March 2026) remains elevated but without a physical cut materializing.
items.fact: Pakistan's PTA reported on July 2, 2026 that 'a fault in the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system' was causing 'intermittent degradation in service quality and connectivity,' with Transworld Associates coordinating with the SMW5 consortium to identify the root cause; the fault was not yet characterized as a confirmed full severing. Source: Dawn.com / PTA statement, July 2, 2026.

dissent.view: Capacity Media (March 2026) and AGBI (March 2026) characterize the Hormuz cable network as facing a 'credible threat' with 2,500 vessels crowding the strait and 250 untraceable ships — some analysts argue this constitutes a persistent elevated-threat environment closer to a level-2 precursor.

September 2025 Red Sea cuts to SMW4 and IMEWE near Jeddah were confirmed physical severings causing multi-country disruption; if still unrepaired by July 2026, this would be level 2, but historical repair timelines (2–5 months) strongly suggest restoration before July 2026.

items.label: AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires confirmed curtailment of data-center load, a declared grid emergency, or a power-scarcity-driven moratorium; all three criteria are met simultaneously: DOE/PJM emergency curtailment orders were issued and executed in May and July 2026, a grid emergency was declared under Federal Power Act Section 202(c), and New York enacted a first-in-nation statewide data-center moratorium explicitly citing grid capacity stress.
items.fact: DOE issued Section 202(c) emergency orders on June 30, 2026 authorizing PJM Interconnection to curtail data centers with >=50 MW backup generation during July 1-3 heat emergency; PJM forecast record peak of 166,147 MW on July 2 with Maximum Generation and Load Management alerts active (Utility Dive / ElectricChoice, July 2026). Separately, NY Governor Hochul issued Executive Order No. 62 imposing a temporary statewide moratorium on new data centers (governor.ny.gov, ~July 2026), and NY Legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) on June 4, 2026. IEA Electricity 2026 confirms >2,500 GW stalled in global queues and 'many power systems are already experiencing rising congestion-related curtailment' (iea.org, 2026).

dissent.view: FERC June 18, 2026 orders aim to 'significantly shorten the multi-year interconnection queue backlog' - suggesting queues may ease on a 12-24 month horizon, but this is a forward-looking regulatory action, not current relief

LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition shows total active U.S. queue volume fell 10% in 2025 (1,312 GW gen + 749 GW storage), suggesting some queue relief on generation side, though large-load data-center queues remain severe

items.label: China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
items.rationale: The mid-March 2026 addition of NK-blend and expanded phosphate bans constitutes a NEW, broadened restriction beyond prior measures, satisfying rubric level 2 (new or broadened restriction in trailing ~4 months). The partial May urea quota reopening does not lift the phosphate/NK bans nor the overall quota-managed framework, and international urea prices rose ~40% vs pre-war levels confirming physical market impact - corroborating price move is present.
items.fact: In mid-March 2026 Beijing banned exports of nitrogen-potassium fertilizer blends and certain additional phosphate varieties (per Reuters/Bloomberg, March 19-21 2026), layered on top of (a) the NDRC Dec 11 2025 phosphate suspension through August 2026 and (b) existing urea export quotas. By late May 2026 China issued a limited urea quota of ~1.5-1.6M tonnes for June-August with a $660/t price floor (Profercy, May 26 2026), but the phosphate suspension and NK-blend bans remained in force. Sources: potatopro.com (March 23 2026), exiger.com (April 16 2026), profercy.com (May 26 2026), sunsirs.com (Dec 16 2025).

dissent.view: The May 26 2026 urea quota release (~1.5-1.6M t, June-August window) could be read as a partial relaxation of urea restrictions, arguably moving back toward level 1 (in place but unchanged) rather than level 2 tightening, since the March broadening is now slightly outside the strict 3-month trailing window (March 19 vs July 27 = ~4 months).

items.label: Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: A confirmed statewide moratorium has been enacted in New York via a signed executive order with immediate physical effect on permitting, satisfying the rubric's top band ('a statewide moratorium enacted'); >100 local jurisdictions with enacted pauses further exceeds the '>10 jurisdictions' threshold. Jurisdictions with enacted or near-enacted actions include: New York (statewide EO, enacted); Virginia (court-invalidated approvals + 15 enacted bills); Georgia (multiple county moratoria); Maine (legislature passed, governor vetoed); Texas/Hill County (briefly enacted, then rescinded); plus 100+ unnamed local municipalities.
items.fact: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed Executive Order No. 62 on July 14, 2026, imposing the nation's first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale (50 MW+) data center construction by halting DEC discretionary permits for up to one year. Additionally, >100 local municipalities nationwide have adopted data center moratoria and at least 14 states have introduced or considered statewide moratorium legislation. (Primary sources: governor.ny.gov EO #62, July 14 2026; Jones Day / jonesday.com, July 2026)

dissent.view: Maine's legislature passed a moratorium in April 2026 but Gov. Janet Mills vetoed it, so Maine does NOT count as an enacted statewide moratorium.

The NY Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560, passed June 4) has not yet been signed or vetoed by Hochul; EO 62 (July 14) is a narrower executive order rather than enacted statute, and Hochul may veto the broader bill.

items.label: Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)
items.rationale: ICSG officially forecasts a +96,000t surplus for 2026, which exceeds the +100kt surplus threshold in the rubric; this maps mechanically to band 0 (SURPLUS). The surplus figure is above the ±100kt balanced range, so band 1 does not apply.
items.fact: ICSG April 2026 Lisbon meeting forecast: refined copper market surplus of ~96,000 metric tons in 2026, reversing its October 2025 forecast of a 150,000t deficit, attributed to lower-than-expected demand growth (usage now +1.6% vs prior +2.1%) and higher secondary/scrap refined production. Source: ADMIS.com (April 24 2026), Recycling Today (April 28 2026), Metalnomist (July 2026), citing ICSG Copper Market Forecast 2026/2027 document.

dissent.view: October 2025 ICSG forecast (now superseded) projected a 150,000t deficit for 2026 due to mine disruptions at Grasberg/Kamoa constraining concentrate supply
Goldman Sachs base case: 2026 surplus of ~160kt, broadly corroborating ICSG direction but a larger surplus figure

items.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
items.rationale: D3 (extreme drought) confirmed across the US Southwest including Arizona and the Colorado River Basin with reservoir storage at multi-decade record lows — this meets rubric level 2 ('extreme/exceptional D3-D4'). No confirmed fab/farm production curtailment found in 2026, but D3-D4 physical conditions alone satisfy the ACUTE threshold under the rubric.
items.fact: US Drought Monitor (droughtmonitor.unl.edu, released July 21 2026 via drought.gov/current-conditions) shows Arizona at 61.02% D2+, 1.47% D3 (extreme drought) as of June 30 2026, with the USBR reporting Lake Powell at 22% full (34% of average, lowest on record for the date in 30 years) and Lake Mead at 27% full (45% of average) as of July 19 2026 per USBR via coyotegulch.blog July 23 2026; western-water.com (July 18 2026, sourced from USDM July 16 2026) confirms D3/D4 expansion in central Colorado, and Arizona ADWR confirms 'Exceptional (D4) and Extreme (D3) long-term drought was found in every county' (azwater.gov, June 16 2026).

dissent.view: Taiwan: no current active drought or fab water-rationing order found for 2026; background long-term water-stress risk noted but no acute 2026 event confirmed

items.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
items.rationale: Over 5 years = >60 months median IR-to-COD; 60 is the minimum bound implied by the LBNL report and is used as the value since the public highlights give no more precise figure. The trend is confirmed as still increasing relative to prior years.
items.fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (data through end of 2025, published July 1 2026): 'For the regions with available data, the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025.' Source: https://emp.lbl.gov/queues

dissent.view: Enverus (May 2025) reports queue times of 4-9 years depending on region and technology, implying a wider range rather than a single national median

items.label: Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires the strait to be CLOSED (not merely contested) AND a corroborating crude-oil price signal: both conditions are confirmed - zero tanker transits as of 25-26 Jul 2026 and Brent ~$90-97/bbl (~30% above year-ago levels). No signed ceasefire, MOU, or naval convoy operation is in force that would cap the rating at 1; Iran exited the June MOU and resumed attacks, and diplomatic talks with Oman on 26 Jul produced no change in transit conditions.
items.fact: Windward AI (25 Jul 2026): only one vessel (outbound general cargo) transited Hormuz in the 24 hours to 25 July; zero tankers crossed in either direction; zero inbound transits recorded in the same window - traffic down ~90% year-on-year. Straits.live (26 Jul 2026) rates the strait 'effectively closed to commercial shipping.' Brent crude ~$90-97/bbl on 27 Jul 2026, up ~30% year-on-year (TradingEconomics / Fortune, 27 Jul 2026), corroborating physical closure. Persian Gulf supplies ~44% of seaborne sulfur and ~43% of seaborne urea globally (NDSU Ag Trade Monitor, Mar 2026); those flows are halted.

dissent.view: US military stated 'the waterway remains open with American support' (CENTCOM, ~25 Jul 2026), implying a contested-but-not-closed framing that could imply a Level 1 reading

items.label: Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
items.rationale: At 27.03% of capacity, Lake Mead falls below the rubric's 30% CRITICAL threshold, satisfying the primary criterion. Physical impact is confirmed: USBR has declared a Level 1 Shortage Condition, reduced Powell-to-Mead releases accelerating decline, and warned of up to 40% hydropower capacity reduction at Hoover Dam.
items.fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,041.21 feet MSL as of Sat Jul 25 2026, at 27.03% of capacity and 187.79 ft below full pool (1,229 ft); power pool is ~950 ft (~91 ft below current level). Source: lakemead.water-data.com citing USBR data, corroborated by USBR Weekly Hydrologic Update (Jun 29 2026) showing 1,041.81 ft / 27% capacity, and Newsweek/USBR (Jun 18 2026) at 29% of capacity.

items.label: Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Three top-10 copper mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, El Teniente) have confirmed, physically active production cuts in 2026 — meeting the >=3 mines threshold — and multiple major institutions independently forecast a 2026 refined copper market deficit driven by these disruptions, satisfying both prongs of the CLUSTER criterion.
items.fact: Grasberg (world #2) running at ~40-50% capacity as of April/May 2026 with full restart pushed to early 2028 and 2026 output cut to 700M lb from 1.7B lb pre-incident (mining.com, May 8 2026); Kamoa-Kakula still in recovery from 2025 flooding + sulfuric acid shortages (Crux Investor / J.P. Morgan, May 26 2026); El Teniente disruption removing ~25,000t in 2026 (investorideas.com, Feb 12 2026); ICSG cut 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.6% citing DRC, Chile, Indonesia constraints (The Oregon Group, May 11 2026); Morgan Stanley forecasts 600kt 2026 deficit, J.P. Morgan 330kt (Crux Investor, May 26 2026).

items.label: Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: The 1960 IWT is formally suspended/contested — a treaty suspended and officially contested by both parties — with explicit war threats tied to river/dam operations exchanged at the ministerial and military-command level, satisfying rubric band 1 (treaty suspended/contested, official threats exchanged). No confirmed deliberate complete flow cut-off or kinetic action has been documented, so band 2 is not yet triggered despite the Indian water minister's 'not a single drop' rhetoric and accelerating diversion infrastructure.
items.fact: India's Indus Waters Treaty remains formally 'in abeyance' since April 2025; on July 3 2026 India's MEA reaffirmed the freeze; Pakistan's Defence Minister stated 'the moment we feel our national security is under threat... we will go to war'; Pakistan's Corps Commanders Conference (July 6) formally backed water-security red lines; Pakistan addressed the UN Security Council on July 23-24 warning against 'weaponisation of water'. India has stopped sharing hydrological data and is fast-tracking Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel construction, but no confirmed complete physical cut-off of flow is documented. (Sources: CNBC June 22 2026; The Diplomat July 7 2026; Eurasia Review July 24 2026; nation.com.pk July 24 2026; National Interest July 2026)

dissent.view: India frames its position narrowly as withdrawing 'cooperative goodwill' while leaving physical flow intact, arguing no actual cut-off has occurred (National Interest, July 2026)

Pakistan's Deputy PM and UN Ambassador assert the IWT remains 'valid, binding and operative' and that India's abeyance is illegal, implying the treaty is not truly suspended in Pakistan's legal reading (The Hindu / nation.com.pk, June-July 2026)

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric's level-2 criterion is 'deadline missed without final rules' — exactly what occurred on July 18, 2026, with all five mandated agencies still in proposed/comment stage and no final rule published. No court stay was required to satisfy level 2; the plain missed deadline with zero finalized rules is sufficient.
items.fact: The GENIUS Act's statutory rulemaking deadline of July 18, 2026 was missed: Treasury, OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, and NCUA collectively issued 10 NPRMs but zero final implementing rules by that date; the FinCEN/CIP comment window alone runs through August 21, 2026. Source: multiple corroborating reports (BigGo Finance, CryptoDaily, GNCrypto, CoinTribune) dated July 18-27, 2026; OCC NPRM bulletin occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-3.html; FDIC NPRM fdic.gov FIL dated April 2026.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The >25bps yield rise on fiscal news triggers score=1 under the rubric; however, auctions are clearing well above the disorderly threshold (4.55x vs <2 floor) and no emergency BOJ operation has been reported, ruling out score=2.
items.fact: 10y JGB yield hit 2.82% on July 24, 2026 (TradingEconomics/Reuters), up ~+70bps from ~2.1% in March 2026, explicitly driven by Takaichi fiscal concerns per Oxford Economics (June 12, 2026); the most recent 30y auction (July 7, 2026) cleared with a bid-to-cover of 4.55x (MOF/Dukascopy, July 7, 2026); June supplementary budget (~3 trn yen) financing path disputed — Takaichi promised flat net issuance but deficit bonds will be used and experts call the math questionable (CNBC, June 1, 2026).

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: YTD insured losses of ~$46-47bn are ~28% BELOW the 10-year average of ~$64bn for H1, and no single event exceeded $5bn — both conditions satisfy the NORMAL rubric (YTD <= 10y average AND no single event >$10bn). The hurricane season is below-average due to El Niño, and H2 has not yet produced a major landfalling storm or large wildfire loss.
items.fact: Global insured catastrophe losses totaled $47bn in H1 2026 per Aon, and at least $46bn per Gallagher Re — 28% below the 10-year H1 average of ~$64bn. The largest single event (U.S. SCS outbreak April 23-29) generated ~$5bn in insured losses, well below the $10bn single-event threshold. Source: Aon Global Catastrophe Recap H1 2026 (Artemis, ~July 22 2026); Gallagher Re Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report H1 2026 (Risk & Insurance, ~July 22 2026).

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Three actual notch-cuts by the Big Three agencies all occurred within the trailing 12-month window ending 2026-07-27, satisfying rubric level 2 unambiguously. No agency currently holds France on negative watch alone without an accompanying recent cut.
items.fact: Fitch cut France from AA- to A+ on ~13 Sep 2025 (stable outlook); S&P cut France from AA- to A+ on ~17 Oct 2025 (stable outlook, reaffirmed 30 May 2026); Moody's cut France from Aa2 to Aa3 in Dec 2024 (stable outlook, then negative outlook Oct 2025). All three cuts fall within the trailing 12 months from 2026-07-27. Sources: spglobal.com (Oct 2025, May 2026), fitchratings.com via CNBC/Euronews (Sep 2025), moodys.com via France24/Reuters (Dec 2024, Oct 2025).

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: The truce is formally intact but partially breached: China's April-2025 licensing regime was explicitly excluded from the truce and volume data corroborate ongoing throttling of heavy REE shipments. With the nominal Nov-10-2026 expiry now ~106 days away and no renewal confirmed, the indicator sits at '1 - EXPIRING/fraying' due to the documented partial breach rather than the day-count alone.
items.fact: The Nov-10-2025 US-China minerals truce (suspending China's Oct-9-2025 controls through Nov-10-2026) remained formally in force as of mid-May 2026 per a senior US official (E&E News/Reuters, May 12-13 2026), but Chinese customs data showed heavy rare-earth exports (yttrium, dysprosium, terbium) still down ~50% since April-2025 controls — which were never suspended — and ITI Council (May 7, 2026) reported 'Chinese export licenses are often delayed or denied'; no formal extension was announced at the May 2026 Trump-Xi summit (CFR, May 15, 2026).

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials and USA Rare Earth) are on MOFCOM's export control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying rubric level 1 exactly. Multiple primary sources explicitly characterise the action as entity-specific rather than a blanket/categorical ban on the US rare-earth sector, and the muted equity price reaction corroborates the absence of a sector-wide shock required for level 2.
items.fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to its export control list under the Export Control Law and Dual-Use Items regulations; the two US rare-earth producers MP Materials Corp and USA Rare Earth are explicitly listed alongside 8 defence-sector firms. The measure is entity-specific, not a sector-wide or categorical ban on US rare-earth producers as a class. Source: Global Times / MOFCOM spokesperson statement, 22 June 2026 (https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202606/1364081.shtml); corroborated by Benchmark Minerals (25 June 2026), Al Jazeera (22 June 2026), Bloomberg (22 June 2026). Market signal: MP Materials share price was roughly flat and USA Rare Earth modestly higher on announcement day, consistent with entity-specific rather than sector-wide shock.

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: YoY the index remains elevated (+2.2%), disqualifying a FALLING rating; MoM change is only -0.3% (well inside the ±3% ELEVATED band), and neither the MoM (+5%) nor 3-month (+10%) thresholds for SPIKING are breached.
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 130.3 points in June 2026, down 0.3% MoM from May but 2.2% above its year-earlier level. Source: FAO newsroom (fao.org), released 3 July 2026.

flags.name: Redemption gates widespread, but HY spreads benign
flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.
